title: Happy-Go-Lucky
full_review:
What if you decided that, no matter what terrible people or misfortune you were to encounter each day, absolutely nothing would dampen your cheerful optimism?

So it is with Poppy (Sally Hawkins), the persistently good-natured grade schoolteacher and unconventional heroine of British writer-director Mike Leigh's "Happy-Go-Lucky" (Miramax).

Throughout the film, set in London, 30-year-old Poppy interacts with her unique circle of friends, relatives and acquaintances: her longtime roommate and fellow schoolteacher, Zoe (Alexis Zegerman); her tightly wound driving instructor, Scott (Eddie Marsan); an impassioned flamenco trainer (Karina Fernandez); her sister, Suzy (Kate O'Flynn); and her embittered pregnant sister, Helen (Caroline Martin).

Though never dull, the film is occasionally static with Leigh's trademark improvisational methods evident in the naturalistic but often astute dialogue, while Poppy's mannerisms -- including a particularly annoying laugh -- can frequently be grating.

Yet as it unreels, the movie builds in interest and its heroine's eccentricities become increasingly understandable and even admirable. On the way home from work, for instance, she meets an erratic homeless man and, even at the seeming risk of her safety, tries to make a connection. They do finally share a magical moment of lucidity before he retreats into his private unbalanced world again.

We also observe her empathetic handling of a young bully in the classroom. With the help of the school's social worker, Tim (Samuel Roukin), they learn of the boy's troubled home life (and in the process, incidentally, fall in love). Finally, in a decidedly serious confrontation with the unbalanced, deeply angry Scott, we understand most completely how Poppy's surface gaiety and unshakable optimism are aspects of a profound respect for life and human dignity.

Hawkins won the Berlin Film Festival best actress award and, her character's sometimes annoying eccentricities notwithstanding, she gives a finely shaded performance. But the cast is uniformly good, with Marsan's scene-stealing Scott especially impressive, his comic persona morphing scarily into dangerous paranoia.

The film is poignant and often amusing, and like its heroine admirably compassionate in its worldview.

The film contains some rough language and brief profanity, some crude expressions and sexual remarks, and an implied nonmarital sexual encounter. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
